newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tax adviser says Steffi Graf aware of tax scheme.
newsitem.headline: Tax adviser says Steffi Graf aware of tax scheme.

text.p: A former family tax advisor to tennis star Steffi Graf told a court on Friday she was fully aware of a complex scheme designed to keep German tax collectors away from her earnings.

Joachim Eckardt, on trial alongside Graf's father Peter for tax evasion, told the court that despite her claims to the contrary, Steffi Graf had long known that large amounts of her tournament winnings and sponsorship money were being concealed.
"Even Steffi knew about the details of what was going on since the middle of 1991," Eckardt testified, directly contradicting remarks made by Peter Graf on the trial's opening day on Thursday.
Peter Graf, who has spent the last 13 months in custody and faces a 10-year jail sentence if convicted, said he had kept his daughter in the dark about her finances.
Steffi Graf, the world's number one, has reached the semi-finals of the U.S. Open tennis tournament and is aiming to win her 31st Grand Slam title this weekend in New York.

Her father, a 58-year-old former used car salesman, told the court on Thursday he had once been close to moving his family abroad to avoid high taxes but decided to stay because local political leaders had assured him of tax relief for his daughter.

Prosecutors allege Graf and Eckardt failed to declare to authorities 42 million marks ($28 million) worth of income between 1989 and 1993 and failed to pay 19 million marks ($13 million) in taxes from the late 1980s.
Eckardt, who has spent the last 11 months in custody, is also facing a tax evasion conviction. The two men have separate defence teams but are being tried at the same time.

Eckardt testified on Friday that Steffi Graf had been informed about a plan through which her tournament winnings and sponsorship income was paid into a holding company in Amsterdam known as Sunpark as a way of avoiding high German taxes.

"The entire operation, the way it was set up and the amounts from the sponsors involved, were openly discussed," Eckardt said, adding that Peter Graf, his wife Heidi, and Steffi were present at the meeting.
Asked by the court whether the family was aware the scheme was questionable from a tax standpoint, he replied: "That was obvious."
The hirsute Eckardt described how Peter Graf had often picked up appearance money from German tennis tournaments in cash sacks and carried it to the Netherlands.
"There was always more money there than what was taxed," Eckardt said. "Of course we knew that we had to turn this "black money' into "white money'."
The money was "pushed back and forth, and stored in different countries", he said.
He described how the Sunpark holding company in Amsterdam was quickly liquidated in mid-1995 immediately after authorities raided the Graf house in Bruehl.
"The money -- I can't remember the exact amount -- was transferred in four or five chunks to some island somewhere," Eckardt said.
